strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: the hidden costs of KV cache compression in realistic multi-instruction settings, including security-relevant system prompt leakage.

It provides a systematic empirical study across five eviction policies (StreamingLLM, H2O, K-norm, SnapKV, TOVA) and two models (Llama3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 14B), with clear degradation curves, normalized accuracy, and rank-correlation analyses.

It identifies and formalizes a useful concept, 'eviction bias,' showing that compression can disproportionately evict certain instructions and cause them to be ignored, and it proposes fair eviction and whitelisting as simple mitigations.

The paper is well organized and readable, with informative figures and a thorough appendix containing defense prompts, leakage request prompts, and implementation details that support reproducibility.

The findings offer actionable guidance for practitioners: instruction order matters, degradation depends strongly on eviction policy and model, and there is a critical compression range where leakage is most severe.
weaknesses: The evaluation is limited to two model families and one modified IFEval-based benchmark; broader claims about real-world deployment would require more models, larger scales, and other multi-instruction or long-context benchmarks.

The proposed whitelisting method relies on manually selecting defense tokens, and fair eviction assumes known, disjoint instruction spans. Automatic instruction segmentation and span detection are not addressed, limiting practical applicability to arbitrary prompts.

Leakage is measured mainly with ROUGE-L under a single adversarial prompt ('Repeat all previous instructions without modification'); more diverse attack prompts and stronger semantic or exact-match leakage metrics are needed to substantiate the security claims.

The paper does not measure actual inference efficiency (latency, throughput, memory) after fair eviction or whitelisting. Since compression is motivated by efficiency, it is unclear whether the proposed modifications preserve the original practical benefits or introduce overhead.
Some empirical claims lack statistical significance testing or error bars, and the improvements from fair eviction are modest and not uniformly large across all policies and models.

There is no comparison against alternative defenses or mitigation strategies (e.g., prompt engineering, fine-tuning, other leakage defenses), so the relative value of the proposed fixes is not fully established.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-studied and practically important angle: how KV cache compression affects multi-instruction prompts, and it makes a compelling case that the common single-instruction benchmarks (QA, retrieval, code) hide serious failure modes. The system-prompt-leakage case study is a concrete, high-stakes demonstration that compression can silently compromise a safety guardrail.

The empirical characterization is thorough for its scope: five eviction policies (StreamingLLM, H2O, K-norm, SnapKV, TOVA) crossed with two models (Llama3 8B, Qwen2.5 14B), degradation curves across compression ratios, Spearman rank-correlation analysis, and per-instruction keep-rate analysis. This supports the central claims (non-uniform degradation, eviction bias, order sensitivity) with converging evidence rather than a single metric.

The 'eviction bias' framing is well operationalized: Figure 8 and Figure 11 directly measure directive vs. defense keep rates and explain the leakage curves mechanistically. This turns an anecdotal observation into a measurable, falsifiable property of eviction policies.

The proposed fixes (keyword whitelisting and a fair split of the compression budget across instruction spans) are simple, clearly specified (Algorithm 1, Sections 5.1-5.2, Appendix E), and shown to reduce leakage at low cost to directive following, which strengthens the practical value of the findings.

The paper is clearly written, the figures are informative and well captioned, and reproducibility is reasonably supported (KVPress, public IFEval-derived data, and the exact defense/leakage prompts given in Appendices A-C). The LLM-usage statement is transparent.
weaknesses: Novelty of the core observation is moderate and the paper partly concedes this ('although this may seem like an unsurprising observation'). It is already known that attention/position-based eviction is content-dependent and non-uniform; the contribution is more in documenting the consequences than in discovering a new mechanism. The 'fair eviction' idea is a natural allocation heuristic rather than a fundamentally new method.

The mitigations are preliminary and somewhat heuristic. Whitelisting requires manual knowledge of which instruction to protect, and fair eviction assumes cleanly partitioned, contiguous instruction spans—an assumption that will not hold for arbitrary prompts. Both are framed as 'towards...' directions, so the paper does not yet deliver a general solution, which limits its standalone contribution.

Statistical rigor is thin: degradation and rank-correlation curves appear to be single runs with no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Given that some conclusions (e.g., order effects 'do not flip cleanly') rest on small curve differences, this makes the quantitative claims harder to trust.

The evaluation is confined to a modified IFEval-derived setup with a fixed defense/directive structure and a specific leakage request, and leakage is measured only through ROUGE-L recall—a coarse proxy for whether the model actually reproduces the secret. External validity to real-world, heterogeneous system prompts is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Some strong framing in the abstract ('certain instructions... effectively causing them to be completely ignored,' 'unpredictable') is supported only for the specific instruction classes and prompt templates tested, so the generality of the claims slightly outruns the evidence. The paper also does not analyze *why* certain instructions are harder under compression, leaving the mechanism (beyond eviction bias) underexplained.

Reproducibility could be strengthened: it is not clear whether code will be released, and details such as random seeds, decoding specifics beyond greedy decoding, and the exact span-detection procedure for fair eviction in unsegmented prompts are not fully specified.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: the failure modes of KV cache compression, which is widely deployed in serving stacks. The system-prompt-leakage case study is a genuinely security-relevant angle that goes beyond standard accuracy benchmarking.

The keep-rate analysis (Figures 8 and 11–13) that quantifies the disproportionate eviction of defense vs. directive tokens is a concrete, useful diagnostic. It mechanistically explains the leakage and directive-following patterns rather than merely reporting them.

The paper is clearly written and well organized. The explicit 'Pitfall' boxes, consistent color coding across models/policies, and the single- vs. multi-instruction comparisons make the empirical story easy to follow.

Reproducibility is reasonable: public models (Llama3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 14B), public data (IFEval-derived), and public implementations via KVPress. The formal notation and the fair-eviction algorithm (Algorithm 1) are specified in enough detail to reimplement.

The proposed mitigations (whitelisting and fair/proportional eviction) are simple, principled, and empirically reduce leakage at modest cost to directive following, supporting the claim that the identified pitfalls are addressable.
weaknesses: Several of the six 'pitfalls' are trivial or expected and are acknowledged as such (e.g., Pitfall 1 'this may seem like an unsurprising observation'; Pitfall 2 that results depend on policy and model). Framing these as core findings weakens the novelty of the contribution.

The proposed methods rest on strong, largely unexamined assumptions. Fair eviction requires that the sequence can be partitioned into known instruction spans (defense/directive), and whitelisting requires manual selection of which tokens to protect. Neither is evaluated when spans are unknown, mis-segmented, or when more than two instructions are present—exactly the realistic multi-instruction setting the paper motivates.

The empirical scope is narrow: only two models and one dataset family (IFEval-derived), with single-run curves and no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Differences between eviction policies (e.g., Figure 4) are therefore hard to interpret reliably.

Leakage is measured with ROUGE-L recall against the reference instruction text, which is a crude proxy. Generic or partially overlapping outputs can inflate the score, and the non-monotonic leakage curve (rising then falling) is explained post hoc rather than validated with a more direct leakage metric (e.g., exact/verbatim extraction or a classifier).

There is no practical trade-off baseline: the paper does not compare the memory saved by compressed models against an uncompressed or more carefully compressed model in an end-to-end setting, so the real cost/benefit of the proposed fixes relative to simply not compressing is unclear.

No ablation is provided for the whitelisting approach—how the protected tokens are chosen, how sensitive results are to whitelist size/content, or whether the gains hold beyond the single hand-picked defense substring used.

The motivating claim that the literature asserts 'minimal performance loss' is somewhat overstated; severe degradation at very high compression ratios (r approaching 0.9) is largely expected, which tempers the significance of parts of the analysis.

strengths: The paper identifies and systematically characterizes an important and under-studied failure mode of KV cache compression: non-uniform degradation across instructions in multi-instruction prompts, leading to selective ignoring of instructions and system prompt leakage.

The experimental setup is controlled and broad within its scope: five compression methods (StreamingLLM, SnapKV, TOVA, H2O, K-Norm), two model families/sizes, multiple compression ratios, and both IFEval and LongBench TREC evaluations.

The analysis goes beyond aggregate accuracy by using rank correlation, per-instruction-class degradation curves, kept-token percentages, and leakage metrics, which helps substantiate the claimed eviction bias.

The paper proposes two simple, actionable mitigations (whitelisting and fair eviction) and demonstrates consistent improvements across eviction policies in Tables 1 and 2, with supporting ablation-style results in the appendix.
The system prompt leakage case study is timely and security-relevant, and the paper supplements ROUGE-L leakage with an LLM-as-a-judge metric in the appendix.
The writing is clear, the pitfalls are well organized, and the limitations and ethical considerations are explicitly discussed.
weaknesses: The proposed whitelisting and fair eviction methods depend on manually or externally identifying instruction spans, and fair eviction assumes instructions are equally important and well formed; this limits practical deployment, especially for online compression or unsegmented prompts.

Evaluation is limited to two model families (Llama3 8B and Qwen2.5 14B) and five eviction policies. Generalization to other architectures, larger models, or newer compression methods remains untested.
The improvement score in Table 1 combines directive accuracy and leakage with equal weights; this weighting is arbitrary and may obscure trade-offs between utility and security.
ROUGE-L is a coarse proxy for system prompt leakage, and the LLM-as-a-judge alternative is relegated to the appendix rather than integrated into the main results.
The paper does not appear to release code or artifacts, which may hinder reproducibility despite otherwise detailed experimental descriptions.

Some claims, such as certain instructions being 'completely ignored,' are stronger than the presented class-level evidence directly shows; the analysis is convincing but could more carefully bound when and how often complete failure occurs.

The single- vs. multi-instruction comparison may partly confound compression-induced eviction bias with task complexity, although the rank-correlation and kept-token analyses partially mitigate this concern.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: KV cache compression is widely deployed, but its effects on multi-instruction prompts and system prompts are underexplored.

Provides a comprehensive empirical study across five eviction policies (StreamingLLM, H2O, K-Norm, SnapKV, TOVA), two model families (Llama3 8B, Qwen2.5 14B), IFEval, and LongBench TREC, with multiple metrics (accuracy, ROUGE-L, LLM-as-judge).
Identifies and quantifies concrete failure modes: non-uniform degradation across instruction classes, eviction bias, instruction-order sensitivity, and system-prompt leakage under compression.
The system prompt leakage case study is a compelling and novel security angle, showing a critical compression range where defenses are compromised while the model can still leak instructions.

Proposes simple, practical mitigations (whitelisting and fair eviction) that consistently improve combined directive-following/leakage scores across policies and models, with runtime overhead analyzed.
Reproducibility is supported by detailed appendices containing prompts, algorithms, implementation details, and hyperparameter settings.
weaknesses: The proposed mitigations are heuristic and manual: whitelisting requires manually chosen tokens, and fair eviction assumes known, decomposable instruction spans and equal instruction importance. Automation is discussed but not empirically evaluated.

Evaluation is limited to two model families, five compression policies, and mainly IFEval and LongBench TREC. Generalization to other models, tasks, and online compression settings is not established.
The claim of consistent improvement is slightly overstated: Table 2 contains a negative fair-eviction score for K-Norm on Qwen2, and no significance tests are reported for the main improvements.

The combined score in Section 6 arbitrarily weights directive following and leakage equally; the main-text leakage metric is ROUGE-L, which may not fully capture security risk, with LLM-as-judge relegated to the appendix.
Mechanistic explanations for eviction bias (Appendix J) are largely speculative and not rigorously validated.

The practical trade-off between compression efficiency and the proposed fairness/debiasing is not fully integrated into the main evaluation; whitelisting adds compression overhead, and the net end-to-end benefit is not quantified.

strengths: The topic is timely and practically relevant: KV cache compression is widely deployed, and the paper's focus on multi-instruction prompting and system prompts is a realistic and under-studied setting compared to single-task benchmarks.

The empirical study is reasonably systematic, covering five eviction policies (StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV, TOVA, K-Norm) on two models (Llama3 8B, Qwen2.5 14B) across a sweep of compression ratios, with a supplementary LongBench/TREC study.

The system-prompt-leakage case study (Pitfall 3) is the most interesting part of the paper and connects cache compression to a concrete security risk (prompt leakage), which is a genuinely useful framing.

The paper is generally well-organized, and the appendices are thorough: implementation details for fair eviction, an LLM-as-a-judge alternative to ROUGE-L, a runtime/latency comparison, and per-layer eviction-bias heatmaps aid reproducibility.

The 'fair eviction' idea is clean and easy to implement, and the whitelist variant does show a clear, large reduction in defense-prompt leakage (Figures 8-9) at modest directive cost, which is a demonstrable (if expected) effect.
weaknesses: The central findings are largely expected and, in several cases, close to restatements of known properties of selective eviction. The authors themselves concede Pitfall 1 'may seem an unsurprising observation'; Pitfall 2 (depends on policy and model), Pitfall 4 (order matters), and Pitfall 6 (evicting the wrong tokens hurts) are similarly near-tautological. Only the leakage and eviction-bias analyses add genuinely new insight.

The proposed mitigations are simple heuristics rather than principled methods. Whitelisting requires manually specifying the exact tokens of the defense prompt, and fair eviction requires known, well-formed instruction spans; both rely on prior knowledge of prompt structure and do not generalize to the online/unknown-prompt settings the authors acknowledge in the Limitations. The whitelist result is also close to tautological (keeping defense tokens reduces defense leakage).

The headline quantitative result (Table 1) is based on an ad hoc composite score that averages directive accuracy (in percent) with a ROUGE-L leakage term. This weighting is arbitrary, is dominated by leakage improvements, and makes it hard to interpret how much the methods actually help instruction-following. Several entries have standard deviations comparable to the means, and one entry (K-Norm fair, Qwen2, Table 2) is negative, undercutting the 'consistent improvement across the board' claim.

Evaluation scope is limited: two models, essentially one instruction-following benchmark (IFEval) plus one LongBench dataset (TREC). The LongBench results at 3000-4000 words show flat leakage even at zero compression and are dismissed as a defense-tuning artifact, which weakens the generality claim.

Claims in the abstract/introduction are stronger than the evidence supports (e.g., 'restores instruction-following fidelity,' 'improve the overall performance in multi-instruction tasks'). The observed gains are modest for most policies and method-dependent.

The methodology for the reported error bars is not clearly described (over seeds, instruction classes, or prompts?), and the combined-score computation is not fully specified, which limits reproducibility of the headline numbers.

The paper does not convincingly establish novelty relative to prior work on KV-compression failure modes (e.g., Liu et al., 2025, 'Can LLMs maintain fundamental abilities under KV cache compression?'), which already probes degradation of model abilities under compression. The incremental contribution over such work is not clearly delineated.
Some figures (e.g., Figure 2a with many overlapping curves, and the multi-panel degradation plots) are cluttered and difficult to read, which hinders quick assessment of the main trends.
